items.stem: Complete the statement: Earnings per share is calculated as …
options: profit before tax ÷ number of ordinary shares
profit for the year attributable to ordinary shareholders ÷ number of ordinary shares in issue
dividends paid ÷ number of ordinary shares
items.answer: profit for the year attributable to ordinary shareholders ÷ number of ordinary shares in issue
items.markingKey: EPS = (profit after tax − preference dividends) / ordinary shares [1].

items.stem: Explain why a high dividend cover may be viewed both favourably and unfavourably by shareholders.
items.answer: Favourably: dividends are secure and profits are retained for growth. Unfavourably: shareholders seeking income receive a small proportion of profit as dividend.
items.markingKey: Security/retention [1]; low payout for income investors [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why preference dividends are deducted before calculating EPS.
items.answer: EPS measures earnings available to ordinary shareholders; preference dividends are paid first and are not available to them.
items.markingKey: EPS for ordinary shareholders [1]; preference paid first [1] [2]

items.stem: Saffron plc has 1,000,000 ordinary shares of $1.00 each in issue and $250,000 5% preference shares. Profit for the year after tax was $888,000. An ordinary dividend of $0.35 per share was paid and the market price of an ordinary share is $17.51. Calculate the earnings per share and the price/earnings ratio.
items.answer: EPS 87.55 cents; P/E 20.0

items.stem: Sunbird plc has 4,900,000 ordinary shares of $0.25 each in issue and $200,000 5% preference shares. Profit for the year after tax was $1,355,000. An ordinary dividend of $0.08 per share was paid and the market price of an ordinary share is $4.12. Calculate the earnings per share, P/E ratio, dividend cover and dividend yield.
items.answer: EPS 27.45 cents; P/E 15.0; dividend cover 3.43 times; dividend yield 1.94%

items.stem: Lynx Ltd has 3,100,000 ordinary shares of $1.00 each in issue and $300,000 8% preference shares. Profit for the year after tax was $192,000. An ordinary dividend of $0.02 per share was paid and the market price of an ordinary share is $0.98. Calculate the earnings per share, P/E ratio, dividend cover and dividend yield.
items.answer: EPS 5.42 cents; P/E 18.1; dividend cover 2.71 times; dividend yield 2.04%

items.stem: An adviser is comparing two listed companies for a young investor seeking long-term growth. Marula plc: profit after tax $218,000, preference dividends $5,000, 3,400,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.04, market price $0.75. Sunbird plc: profit after tax $521,000, preference dividends $15,000, 2,800,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.11, market price $1.45. (a) Calculate the EPS and P/E ratio for each company. (b) State two limitations of basing the decision only on these ratios.
items.answer: (a) Marula plc: 6.26 cents, 12.0; Sunbird plc: 18.07 cents, 8.0 (b) Based on past results; share prices fluctuate; different accounting policies; ignores non-financial factors such as management quality and industry outlook.

items.stem: An adviser is comparing two listed companies for an investor who wants a balance of income and growth. Kauri Ltd: profit after tax $466,000, preference dividends $12,500, 4,600,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.02, market price $0.79. Galaxy Ltd: profit after tax $849,000, preference dividends $4,000, 3,600,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.12, market price $3.52. (a) Calculate the dividend cover and dividend yield for each company. (b) State two limitations of basing the decision only on these ratios.
items.answer: (a) Kauri Ltd: 4.93 times, 2.53%; Galaxy Ltd: 1.96 times, 3.41% (b) Based on past results; share prices fluctuate; different accounting policies; ignores non-financial factors such as management quality and industry outlook.

items.stem: Complete the statement: The price/earnings ratio is …
options: earnings per share ÷ market price per share
market price per share ÷ earnings per share
items.answer: market price per share ÷ earnings per share

items.stem: Complete the statement: Dividend yield is …
options: dividend per share ÷ market price per share × 100
items.answer: dividend per share ÷ market price per share × 100

items.stem: Explain one limitation of using the P/E ratio to compare two companies.
items.answer: It depends on share price, which reflects market sentiment, and on EPS, which depends on accounting policies; companies in different industries have different typical P/E ratios.

items.stem: Sunbird plc has 3,100,000 ordinary shares of $0.25 each in issue and $250,000 5% preference shares. Profit for the year after tax was $953,000. An ordinary dividend of $0.21 per share was paid and the market price of an ordinary share is $1.82. What is the earnings per share?
items.answer: 30.34 cents

items.stem: An adviser is comparing two listed companies for an investor who wants a balance of income and growth. Condor Ltd: profit after tax $148,000, preference dividends $4,000, 600,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.17, market price $4.32. Kestrel plc: profit after tax $572,000, preference dividends $6,000, 3,000,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.11, market price $1.51. Calculate the dividend cover and dividend yield for each company.
items.answer: Condor Ltd: 1.41 times, 3.94%; Kestrel plc: 1.72 times, 7.28%

items.stem: Complete the statement: A company is described as highly geared when …
options: a large proportion of its capital comes from fixed-return finance such as loans and preference shares
it has a large amount of inventory
items.answer: a large proportion of its capital comes from fixed-return finance such as loans and preference shares
items.markingKey: High gearing: debt + preference shares large relative to equity [1].

items.stem: Explain why lenders are concerned about a company's gearing and interest cover.
items.answer: High gearing and low interest cover mean a greater risk that the company cannot pay interest or repay loans if profits fall; lenders may demand security or higher rates.
items.markingKey: Risk of default [1]; low cover means little margin [1]; consequence [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why ordinary shareholders might benefit from high gearing when profits are rising.
items.answer: Interest is fixed, so extra profit above the interest cost belongs to the shareholders, raising EPS and return on equity more than in proportion.

items.stem: Horizon plc: ordinary share capital $1,050,000, reserves $1,050,000, 5% debentures $600,000. Profit from operations is $427,000. Calculate the gearing ratio and the interest cover.
items.answer: Gearing 22.2%; interest cover 14.2 times

items.stem: Tamarind Ltd: ordinary share capital $300,000, reserves $670,000, 6% debentures $1,400,000, redeemable preference shares $400,000. Profit from operations is $237,000. Calculate the gearing ratio and the interest cover.
items.answer: Gearing 65.0%; interest cover 2.8 times

items.stem: Extracts for Lynx Ltd: year 2025: equity $500,000, debentures $200,000, profit from operations $294,000, interest $12,000. Year 2026: equity $500,000, debentures $1,250,000, profit from operations $135,000, interest $100,000. (a) Calculate the interest cover for each year. (b) Calculate the return on capital employed (profit from operations ÷ (equity + debentures)) for each year.

A student calculated the gearing of Nimbus plc as 66.7% and said the company is "highly geared". The company has non-current loans of $900,000 and equity of $1,350,000. Using the formula debt ÷ (debt + equity), explain the error and calculate the correct gearing.
items.answer: The student used debt ÷ equity. Correct gearing = $900,000 / $2,250,000 × 100 = 40.0%, which is low/moderate (below 50%).
items.markingKey: Identifies formula used [1]; correct 40.0% [1]; conclusion on level [1] [3]

items.stem: Sirocco plc: ordinary share capital $750,000, reserves $1,060,000, 7% debentures $1,000,000. Profit from operations is $119,000. Calculate the gearing ratio and the interest cover.
items.answer: Gearing 35.6%; interest cover 1.7 times

items.stem: Saffron plc: ordinary share capital $1,950,000, reserves $730,000, 8% debentures $350,000, redeemable preference shares $350,000. Profit from operations is $126,000. Calculate the gearing ratio and the interest cover. The company plans to borrow a further $300,000 at 8%. Recalculate both ratios (assume profit is unchanged) and comment.
items.answer: Gearing 20.7% → 27.2%; interest cover 4.5 → 2.4 times; risk to lenders and shareholders increases

items.stem: Complete the statement: Return on capital employed (ROCE) is calculated as …
items.answer: profit from operations ÷ capital employed × 100

items.stem: Explain two limitations of using ratio analysis to compare two companies.
items.answer: Different accounting policies (depreciation, inventory valuation); different year ends or sizes; historical data; window dressing; ratios do not explain causes.

items.stem: Explain why a fall in the gross margin might occur even though revenue has increased.
items.answer: Prices may have been cut to increase sales volume, or purchase costs may have risen faster than selling prices, or the sales mix changed to lower-margin products.

items.stem: Extracts for Horizon plc for the year ended 31 July 2025: revenue $1,560,000, cost of sales $936,000, expenses $404,000, opening inventory $89,000, closing inventory $148,000, trade receivables $139,000, cash $13,000, trade payables (the only current liability) $221,000, capital employed $2,121,000. Calculate the trade payables turnover in days (purchases = cost of sales + closing − opening inventory), current ratio.
items.answer: trade payables turnover in days 81 days; current ratio 1.36:1
items.markingKey: trade payables turnover in days: $221,000/$995,000 × 365 = 81 days [1]; current ratio: $300,000/$221,000 = 1.36:1 [1]

items.stem: Extracts for Odyssey plc for the year ended 30 September 2025: revenue $1,710,000, cost of sales $1,111,500, expenses $389,000, opening inventory $30,000, closing inventory $117,000, trade receivables $122,000, cash $21,000, trade payables (the only current liability) $102,000, capital employed $1,014,000. Calculate the gross margin, liquid (acid test) ratio, profit margin (profit from operations ÷ revenue).
items.answer: gross margin 35.0%; liquid 1.40:1; profit margin 12.3%

items.stem: The following data is available for the managing director assessing performance. Banyan Ltd: revenue $2,960,000, gross profit $1,332,000, profit from operations $422,000, capital employed $1,399,000, current assets $328,000 (inventory $180,000), current liabilities $238,000, trade receivables $128,000. Horizon plc: revenue $2,100,000, gross profit $945,000, profit from operations $338,000, capital employed $2,758,000, current assets $234,000 (inventory $174,000), current liabilities $32,000, trade receivables $43,000. (a) Calculate the gross margin and ROCE for each company. (b) Calculate the trade receivables collection period for each company (all sales on credit).
items.answer: (a) Banyan Ltd: 45.0%, 30.2%; Horizon plc: 45.0%, 12.3% (b) Banyan Ltd: 16 days; Horizon plc: 7 days

items.stem: Explain why a very high current ratio is not necessarily good.
items.answer: It may indicate excess inventory, slow-paying receivables or idle cash that could be invested more profitably.

items.stem: Extracts for Sirocco plc for the year ended 31 March 2025: revenue $2,850,000, cost of sales $1,425,000, expenses $933,000, opening inventory $186,000, closing inventory $177,000, trade receivables $395,000, cash $51,000, trade payables (the only current liability) $288,000, capital employed $2,548,000. Calculate the return on capital employed, trade receivables turnover in days (all sales on credit).
items.answer: return on capital employed 19.3%; trade receivables turnover in days 51 days
items.markingKey: return on capital employed: $492,000/$2,548,000 × 100 = 19.3% [1]; trade receivables turnover in days: $395,000/$2,850,000 × 365 = 51 days [1]

items.stem: The following data is available for a supplier deciding whether to offer 60 days' credit. Kauri Ltd: revenue $610,000, gross profit $213,500, profit from operations $47,500, capital employed $483,000, current assets $180,000 (inventory $67,000), current liabilities $120,000, trade receivables $77,000. Quetzal plc: revenue $2,820,000, gross profit $846,000, profit from operations $206,000, capital employed $632,000, current assets $408,000 (inventory $56,000), current liabilities $145,000, trade receivables $336,000. (a) Calculate the gross margin and ROCE for each company. (b) Calculate the trade receivables collection period for each company (all sales on credit).
items.answer: (a) Kauri Ltd: 35.0%, 9.8%; Quetzal plc: 30.0%, 32.6% (b) Kauri Ltd: 46 days; Quetzal plc: 43 days

items.stem: Complete the statement: Window dressing means …
options: arranging transactions near the year end to make the financial statements look better than they are
preparing statements in a standard format
items.answer: arranging transactions near the year end to make the financial statements look better than they are

items.stem: Explain two limitations of published financial statements for a potential investor.
items.answer: They are historical and may not predict the future; they omit non-financial factors (staff skills, brand, environment); based on estimates and policies chosen by directors; inflation distorts comparisons.

items.stem: Explain why an accountant faces an ethical dilemma when a director asks for profits to be "smoothed".
items.answer: Smoothing misleads users and breaches integrity and objectivity, but the accountant may fear losing his job or the director's goodwill; he should refuse and, if necessary, report through proper channels.
items.markingKey: Breach of principle [1]; pressure/conflict [1]; appropriate action [1] [3]

items.stem: Before the year end Kestrel plc has current assets of $434,000 (including inventory $122,000) and current liabilities of $195,000. On the last day of the year it uses $157,000 of cash to pay trade payables. Calculate the current ratio before and after, and explain why this may be window dressing.
items.answer: Current ratio 2.23:1 → 7.29:1; it improves the reported position without changing the underlying liquidity, which may mislead users.

items.stem: Before the year end Condor Ltd has current assets of $480,000 (including inventory $159,000) and current liabilities of $273,000. On the last day of the year it uses $98,000 of cash to pay trade payables. Calculate the current ratio before and after, and explain why this may be window dressing.
items.answer: Current ratio 1.76:1 → 2.18:1; it improves the reported position without changing the underlying liquidity, which may mislead users.

items.stem: The draft profit of Marula plc is $378,000, below the $391,000 needed for directors' bonuses. The sales director proposes: (1) delaying recognition of $10,000 of maintenance costs until next year; (2) cutting the allowance for irrecoverable debts by $19,500; (3) paying $64,000 of trade payables from cash on the last day of the year. Current assets are $365,000 and current liabilities $255,000 before (3). (a) Calculate the current ratio before and after proposal (3). (b) Explain how users of the financial statements could be misled.
items.answer: (a) 1.43 → 1.58 (b) Investors overestimate profit and dividends capacity; lenders misjudge liquidity; future profits will fall when costs are recognised.

items.stem: Explain how inflation can limit the usefulness of financial statements.
items.answer: Assets at historical cost may be understated; revenue growth may be due to price rises not volume; comparisons over years become distorted.

items.stem: The directors' report of Meridian Ltd states: "Revenue grew 10% from $930,000 to $1,023,000 — an excellent year." Prices in the economy rose by 14% over the year. Calculate the revenue in real terms (at last year's prices) and the real growth rate, and comment on the directors' statement.
items.answer: Real revenue $897,368; real growth -3.5%; the claim overstates performance because part of the growth is inflation.
items.markingKey: $1,023,000 / 1.14 = $897,368 [1]; real growth -3.5% [1]; comment: inflation limits usefulness of historical figures [1]

items.stem: The draft profit of Galaxy Ltd is $307,000, below the $333,000 needed for directors' bonuses. The sales director proposes: (1) delaying recognition of $38,000 of maintenance costs until next year; (2) cutting the allowance for irrecoverable debts by $18,500; (3) paying $75,000 of trade payables from cash on the last day of the year. Current assets are $339,000 and current liabilities $207,000 before (3). (a) Calculate the profit if proposals (1) and (2) are adopted, and state whether the bonus target is met. (b) Calculate the current ratio before and after proposal (3).
Complete the statement: Dividend cover measures …
options: how quickly the company pays its dividends
how many times the ordinary dividend could be paid out of profit available to ordinary shareholders
the proportion of debt in capital
items.answer: how many times the ordinary dividend could be paid out of profit available to ordinary shareholders
items.markingKey: Cover = profit for ordinary shareholders / ordinary dividends [1].

items.stem: An analyst calculated the EPS of Ibis plc as 39.88 cents, dividing profit after tax of $678,000 by 1,700,000 ordinary shares. The company also has $300,000 8% preference shares. Explain the error and calculate the correct EPS.
items.answer: Preference dividends ($24,000) must be deducted first. Correct EPS = $654,000 / 1,700,000 = 38.47 cents.

items.stem: Quetzal plc has 1,800,000 ordinary shares in issue and no preference shares. Its EPS is 15 cents, its P/E ratio is 8 and its dividend cover is 3 times. Calculate the profit for the year, the market price per share, the total dividend paid and the dividend yield.
items.answer: Profit $270,000; price $1.20; dividends $90,000; yield 4.17%

items.stem: An adviser is comparing two listed companies for a retired teacher seeking regular income. Condor Ltd: profit after tax $847,000, preference dividends $12,500, 3,500,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.17, market price $2.86. Monarch plc: profit after tax $122,000, preference dividends $24,000, 2,400,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.01, market price $0.33. (a) Calculate the dividend cover and dividend yield for each company. (b) State two limitations of basing the decision only on these ratios.
items.answer: (a) Condor Ltd: 1.40 times, 5.94%; Monarch plc: 4.08 times, 3.03% (b) Based on past results; share prices fluctuate; different accounting policies; ignores non-financial factors such as management quality and industry outlook.

items.stem: An adviser is comparing two listed companies for a young investor seeking long-term growth. Equinox plc: profit after tax $389,000, preference dividends $3,000, 2,900,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.04, market price $1.60. Sunbird plc: profit after tax $398,000, preference dividends $16,000, 2,200,000 ordinary shares, ordinary dividend per share $0.12, market price $2.60. (a) Advise the investor which company to choose. (b) State two limitations of basing the decision only on these ratios.
items.answer: (a) For income choose Sunbird plc (higher yield); for growth the market rates Sunbird plc more highly (higher P/E). Recommendation follows the investor's objective; check dividend cover for safety. (b) Based on past results; share prices fluctuate; different accounting policies; ignores non-financial factors such as management quality and industry outlook.
items.markingKey: (a) Links ratios to objective [2]; uses cover/risk [1]; justified recommendation [1] [4] (b) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which is usually included as "debt" when calculating gearing? (b) Complete the statement: A highly geared company that increases profit from operations will see …
items.answer: (a) Redeemable preference shares and debentures (b) a proportionately larger increase in profit available to ordinary shareholders
items.markingKey: (a) Fixed-cost capital: non-current loans, debentures, (redeemable) preference shares [1]. (b) Fixed interest magnifies changes in earnings [1].

items.stem: A student calculated the gearing of Condor Ltd as 42.9% and said the company is "low geared". The company has non-current loans of $450,000 and equity of $1,050,000. Using the formula debt ÷ (debt + equity), explain the error and calculate the correct gearing.
items.answer: The student used debt ÷ equity. Correct gearing = $450,000 / $1,500,000 × 100 = 30.0%, which is low/moderate (below 50%).
items.markingKey: Identifies formula used [1]; correct 30.0% [1]; conclusion on level [1] [3]

items.stem: Condor Ltd: ordinary share capital $1,800,000, reserves $1,250,000, 5% debentures $1,450,000. Profit from operations is $141,000. Calculate the gearing ratio and the interest cover.
items.answer: Gearing 32.2%; interest cover 1.9 times

items.stem: Extracts for Kauri Ltd: year 2024: equity $600,000, debentures $300,000, profit from operations $122,000, interest $18,000. Year 2025: equity $650,000, debentures $750,000, profit from operations $155,000, interest $60,000. (a) Calculate the gearing ratio for each year. (b) Calculate the return on capital employed (profit from operations ÷ (equity + debentures)) for each year.
The trade payables payment period of Equinox plc changed from 48.7 days last year to 78.0 days this year. Explain two possible causes of the change and its significance for the company.
items.answer: The company is taking longer to pay suppliers — perhaps cash shortage; risks losing discounts and supplier goodwill.
items.markingKey: Direction of change interpreted [1]; two plausible causes [2]; significance for stakeholders [1] [4]

items.stem: The rate of inventory turnover of Horizon plc changed from 9.9 times last year to 6.4 times this year. Explain two possible causes of the change and its significance for the company.
items.answer: Inventory is selling more slowly — possible obsolete or excess stock, tying up cash and increasing storage costs.
items.markingKey: Direction of change interpreted [1]; two plausible causes [2]; significance for stakeholders [1] [4]

items.stem: Extracts for Condor Ltd for the year ended 31 December 2025: revenue $1,070,000, cost of sales $695,500, expenses $269,000, opening inventory $125,000, closing inventory $43,000, trade receivables $342,000, cash $28,000, trade payables (the only current liability) $51,000, capital employed $774,000. Calculate the trade payables turnover in days (purchases = cost of sales + closing − opening inventory), rate of inventory turnover (times, using average inventory).
items.answer: trade payables turnover in days 30 days; rate of inventory turnover 8.3 times
items.markingKey: trade payables turnover in days: $51,000/$613,500 × 365 = 30 days [1]; rate of inventory turnover: $695,500/$84,000 = 8.3 times [1]

items.stem: Ana, an accountant at Ibis plc, is asked by a director to value obsolete inventory of $148,000 at cost rather than net realisable value. Explain the ethical principles involved and advise Ana what to do.
items.answer: This breaches integrity and professional competence (IAS 2). Ana should refuse, explain the accounting requirement, record the request and, if pressure continues, raise it with the audit committee or professional body.
items.markingKey: Principle(s): integrity and professional competence (IAS 2) [1]; effect on users of statements [1]; refuse/escalate appropriately [1] [3]

items.stem: The directors' report of Sunbird plc states: "Revenue grew 12% from $1,780,000 to $1,993,600 — an excellent year." Prices in the economy rose by 7% over the year. Calculate the revenue in real terms (at last year's prices) and the real growth rate, and comment on the directors' statement.
items.answer: Real revenue $1,863,178; real growth 4.7%; the claim overstates performance because part of the growth is inflation.
items.markingKey: $1,993,600 / 1.07 = $1,863,178 [1]; real growth 4.7% [1]; comment: inflation limits usefulness of historical figures [1]

items.stem: Before the year end Condor Ltd has current assets of $155,000 (including inventory $20,000) and current liabilities of $258,000. On the last day of the year it uses $43,000 of cash to pay trade payables. Calculate the current ratio before and after, and explain why this may be window dressing.
items.answer: Current ratio 0.60:1 → 0.52:1; it improves the reported position without changing the underlying liquidity, which may mislead users.

items.stem: Complete the statement: A high P/E ratio usually indicates that …
options: investors expect strong future growth in earnings
the company is about to fail
items.answer: investors expect strong future growth in earnings
items.markingKey: Market pays more per $ of current earnings [1].

items.stem: An analyst calculated the EPS of Sunbird plc as 6.15 cents, dividing profit after tax of $246,000 by 4,000,000 ordinary shares. The company also has $50,000 6% preference shares. Explain the error and calculate the correct EPS.
items.answer: Preference dividends ($3,000) must be deducted first. Correct EPS = $243,000 / 4,000,000 = 6.08 cents.

items.stem: Saffron plc has 2,000,000 ordinary shares in issue and no preference shares. Its EPS is 36 cents, its P/E ratio is 10 and its dividend cover is 2 times. Calculate the profit for the year, the market price per share, the total dividend paid and the dividend yield.
items.answer: Profit $720,000; price $3.60; dividends $360,000; yield 5.00%

items.answer: (a) Lynx Ltd: 26.98 cents, 20.0; Marula plc: 6.25 cents, 15.0 (b) Based on past results; share prices fluctuate; different accounting policies; ignores non-financial factors such as management quality and industry outlook.

items.stem: An adviser is comparing two listed companies for an investor who wants a balance of income and growth. items.answer: (a) Horizon plc: 4.02 times, 2.08%; Condor Ltd: 1.66 times, 6.01% (b) Based on past results; share prices fluctuate; different accounting policies; ignores non-financial factors such as management quality and industry outlook.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Complete the statement: A company is described as highly geared when … (b) Complete the statement: A highly geared company that increases profit from operations will see …
items.answer: (a) a large proportion of its capital comes from fixed-return finance such as loans and preference shares (b) a proportionately larger increase in profit available to ordinary shareholders

items.stem: A student calculated the gearing of Delta Ltd as 62.1% and said the company is "highly geared". The company has non-current loans of $900,000 and equity of $1,450,000. Using the formula debt ÷ (debt + equity), explain the error and calculate the correct gearing.

items.stem: Osprey Ltd: ordinary share capital $1,150,000, reserves $530,000, 10% debentures $1,300,000. Profit from operations is $312,000. Calculate the gearing ratio and the interest cover.
items.answer: Gearing 43.6%; interest cover 2.4 times

items.stem: Extracts for Sunbird plc: year 2025: equity $1,300,000, debentures $550,000, profit from operations $250,000, interest $33,000. Year 2026: equity $800,000, debentures $800,000, profit from operations $185,000, interest $64,000. (a) Calculate the gearing ratio for each year. (b) Calculate the interest cover for each year.
The trade receivables collection period of Nimbus plc changed from 38.0 days last year to 61.1 days this year. Explain two possible causes of the change and its significance for the company.
items.answer: Customers are paying more slowly — possible weak credit control or a deliberate policy of longer credit to boost sales; cash flow worsens.
items.markingKey: Direction of change interpreted [1]; two plausible causes [2]; significance for stakeholders [1] [4]

items.stem: The current ratio of Marula plc changed from 1.7:1 last year to 1.0:1 this year. Explain two possible causes of the change and its significance for the company.
items.answer: Liquidity has worsened; current assets now barely cover current liabilities, a risk to paying suppliers on time.

items.stem: Extracts for Nimbus plc for the year ended 30 September 2025: revenue $2,270,000, cost of sales $1,362,000, expenses $703,000, opening inventory $59,000, closing inventory $142,000, trade receivables $62,000, cash $18,000, trade payables (the only current liability) $169,000, capital employed $1,785,000. Calculate the profit margin (profit from operations ÷ revenue), rate of inventory turnover (times, using average inventory).
items.answer: profit margin 9.0%; rate of inventory turnover 13.6 times

items.stem: Sofia, an accountant at Tamarind Ltd, is asked by a director to record $34,000 of sales made in the first week of the next year in the current year. Explain the ethical principles involved and advise Sofia what to do.
items.answer: This breaches integrity (misstatement of revenue). Sofia should refuse, explain the accounting requirement, record the request and, if pressure continues, raise it with the audit committee or professional body.
items.markingKey: Principle(s): integrity (misstatement of revenue) [1]; effect on users of statements [1]; refuse/escalate appropriately [1] [3]

items.stem: Before the year end Quetzal plc has current assets of $455,000 (including inventory $177,000) and current liabilities of $146,000. On the last day of the year it uses $33,000 of cash to pay trade payables. Calculate the current ratio before and after, and explain why this may be window dressing.
items.answer: Current ratio 3.12:1 → 3.73:1; it improves the reported position without changing the underlying liquidity, which may mislead users.

items.stem: The directors' report of Odyssey plc states: "Revenue grew 12% from $1,530,000 to $1,713,600 — an excellent year." Prices in the economy rose by 5% over the year. Calculate the revenue in real terms (at last year's prices) and the real growth rate, and comment on the directors' statement.
items.answer: Real revenue $1,632,000; real growth 6.7%; the claim overstates performance because part of the growth is inflation.
items.markingKey: $1,713,600 / 1.05 = $1,632,000 [1]; real growth 6.7% [1]; comment: inflation limits usefulness of historical figures [1]
